EA2003::152.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required
cases.holding: Section 152(2) and (3) operate at different stages: under s.152(2), where no criminal proceeding has yet been instituted, payment of the compounding sum sets the person at liberty and bars institution of proceedings; s.152(3) (acceptance deemed an acquittal) applies only where a prosecution is already pending. Compounding therefore does not require a pending prosecution.
cases.flag: The judgment refers throughout to 'Section 152(2) of the Electricity Supply Code 2005'; Section 152 is in the Electricity Act, 2003. Recorded, not merged.

EA2003::46.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with Clauses 4.6 & 4.21, Supply Code 2005)
EA2003::46.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation
cases.holding: Under Section 46 a licensee may recover only “expenses reasonably incurred in providing any electric line or electrical plant”, and the burden to prove actual expenditure lies on the licensee (as the Supreme Court's remand directed). Extension of distribution mains and commissioning of new sub-stations is the licensee's own statutory obligation under the first proviso to Section 43(1) and cannot be loaded onto the consumer. On the evidence the 4-pole structure and service line were actually constructed, so Rs. 5,49,181 and Rs. 4,65,000 were rightly retained; the processing fee of Rs. 5,000 is non-refundable per the Cost Data Book.
cases.flag: The Supreme Court's remand order dated 29.11.2022 (in this very case) fixed the frame: refund is to be denied only “to the extent” the respondents prove “the actual expenses incurred.”

EA2003::56(2).topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation
cases.holding: "Sum due" means an amount adjudicated between the parties; un-adjudicated, escalating demands raised years after the service ended are barred.
cases.flag: Respondent pleaded this as "Clause 56(2) of the U.P. Supply Code"; the provision quoted and applied is s.56(2) of the Act. Recorded, not merged.

UP-2005::4.1.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises
cases.holding: No. The arrears-bar in the third proviso to Clause 4.1 applies only to dues on the same 'premises' (Clause 2(ss)); the shop is a distinct premises and the tenant is an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply. Clause 4.3(h) forbids refusal on the ground of dues on other portions; the licensee must instead pursue the defaulters under Clause 4.3(f)(v).

UP-2005::4.21(a).topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised
cases.holding: Yes, refundable. A system-loading charge is a compulsory exaction on one who enjoys the benefit of the distribution system; the liability accrues only once the applicant starts consuming electricity using the licensee's system. A prospective consumer who never takes supply cannot be fastened with it. Refund of Rs. 32,00,000 with interest @ 8.5% p.a. from the date of deposit ordered.

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.holding: No. The clause preserves the charge only till termination and is read subject to the maxim that no party may take advantage of its own wrong. Charges end with actual disconnection (28.9.2007); the demand for January 2008-30.11.2018, with interest, is quashed.

UP-2005::4.3(f).topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises

cases.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.3(f)(i) & (viii) place the duty to ascertain and clear outstanding dues on both seller and purchaser and permit the application to be processed only on clearance. The auction-purchaser, buying 'as-is-where-is', is fixed with 'buyer beware' and cannot escape the statutory charge by relying on the encumbrance-free recital or the vendor's non-consumption.

UP-2005::4.3(g).topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises

cases.title: Anubhav Jaiswal v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises
cases.holding: Only his pro-rata share. Though outstanding dues are the first charge on the premises (Clause 4.3(f)(iv)), on a legal sub-division they are apportioned pro-rata (Clause 4.3(g)) and a connection to the sub-divided portion is given on payment of that portion's share alone (Clause 4.3(h)); the licensee cannot demand the whole. The matter is remanded for fresh pro-rata determination after notice to the original owner.

UP-2005::4.4.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent
cases.holding: Following Seema Mansoor, an occupier (including a tenant) has a statutory right to supply under Sections 42-43 read with Clause 4.4; where the owner's consent is unavailable, the tenant may file an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) to obtain the connection.

UP-2005::5.6(d).topic: Meter-testing procedure vs a compounded theft offence

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Meter-testing procedure vs a compounded theft offence
cases.holding: No. Once the sum is paid under Section 152(1) and the offence is deemed compounded, the tampering stands admitted-compounded and the question of following the meter-testing procedure (para 5.6(d)) does not arise. The theft assessment was made on the Code's formula (Annexure 6.3); the procedural challenge fails.

UP-2005::compounding.topic: Theft (s.135) compounded through the Supply Code — theft/UUE-Code linkage

cases.title: Ajmal v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) compounded through the Supply Code — theft/UUE-Code linkage
cases.holding: The offence of electricity theft under Section 135 being compoundable, the accused's compounding remedy lies 'as provided under the provisions of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005' — the Code furnishing the machinery through which theft (Section 135) and, cognately, unauthorised use of electricity (Section 126) are assessed and compounded. Pending compounding, as the offence does not entail imprisonment beyond seven years, any arrest must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A Cr.P.C.; the FIR, disclosing a cognizable offence, was not quashed.
cases.flag: Scope: the case's express Code engagement is the compounding remedy; the operative relief concerned arrest safeguards (s.41(1)(b)/41-A Cr.P.C.). Retained as a node in the theft / unauthorised-use line, which the Supply Code's assessment and compounding machinery governs.
